title: The Nature of Scientific Thinking in Psychology
description: Understand empiricism, the demarcation problem, why intuition fails, and Popper's falsifiability criterion.

slides.title: Why Common Sense Isn't Science 🧠
slides.content:
# The Limits of Intuition

Many people believe they already understand human psychology simply because they interact with humans every day. However, everyday intuition is riddled with systematic cognitive biases:

* **Hindsight Bias**: The 'I-knew-it-all-along' tendency to view events as having been obvious once they have occurred.
* **Confirmation Bias**: Actively seeking out, remembering, and weighting evidence that supports our existing beliefs while disregarding contradictory data.
* **Overconfidence Effect**: Subjective confidence in judgments reliably exceeding objective accuracy.

To move beyond folk wisdom, psychology relies on **systematic empiricism**—basing conclusions on systematic, verifiable observations of the world rather than casual impressions or authority.

quizData.question: A student claims: 'I knew that couple would break up from the day they met!' despite never saying anything before the breakup. Which cognitive bias is this?
quizData.explanation: Hindsight bias occurs when an outcome appears predictable in retrospect, leading people to believe they foresaw the event all along.

slides.title: Science vs. Pseudoscience ⚖️
slides.content:
## The Demarcation Problem

How do we separate genuine psychological science from pseudoscientific claims like phrenology, biorhythms, or conversion therapy?

| Dimension | Scientific Psychology | Pseudoscience |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Basis of Evidence** | Controlled empirical observation, replicable data | Anecdotal testimonials, personal testimonials |
| **Openness to Revision** | Theories modified or abandoned when disproven | Claims defended with excuses or unfalsifiable loops |
| **Methodology** | Rigorous attempts to disconfirm hypotheses | Selective search for confirming instances |
| **Peer Review** | Scrutinized by independent experts prior to publication | Bypasses peer review, marketed directly to the public |

In real science, findings must be publicly shared, transparently documented, and capable of being independently verified by other researchers.

quizData.question: Which of the following characteristics is a primary hallmark of pseudoscience?

options.text: Undergoing anonymous peer review before publication
Reliance on customer testimonials instead of controlled empirical trials
Willingness to modify hypotheses when data contradict predictions
Publishing raw data and analysis scripts openly

quizData.explanation: Pseudoscience typically relies heavily on anecdotal accounts and emotional testimonials rather than systematically collected, replicable experimental data.

slides.title: Karl Popper & Falsifiability 🛡️
slides.content:
## The Falsifiability Criterion

Philosopher of science **Karl Popper** established that for a theory or claim to be scientific, it must be **falsifiable**.

* A theory is falsifiable if there exists at least one conceivable empirical observation that would prove it wrong.
* If a theory explains every possible outcome after the fact, it actually explains nothing.

For example, if an astrologer claims: 'You will experience either financial gain or a financial lesson this week,' the claim cannot be falsified because every financial event fits the prediction. In contrast, the hypothesis 'Depriving mice of REM sleep for 48 hours will increase latency in learning a Morris water maze by at least 20%' can be clearly supported or refuted.

slides.title: Psychology Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
### Look for the Disconfirming Test

When evaluating any psychological claim, always ask:
> *'What specific observation or experimental result would convince the author that their theory is mistaken?'*

If the author cannot define what evidence would falsify their idea, the claim is a matter of dogma or faith, not psychological science.
